# Introduction

This analysis investigates the evolution of Northern Hemisphere
temperature anomalies using two Gaussian dynamic linear models:
a random walk plus noise model and a local linear trend model.

We estimate variance parameters by maximum likelihood and use
Kalman filtering and smoothing to reconstruct the latent level
and quantify conditional state uncertainty.

Predictive performance is assessed through sequential one-step-ahead
forecasts over the final twenty years, with parameters estimated
on the preceding training sample. The discussion contrasts
continuous latent-state models with the discrete-state
representation used by Hidden Markov Models.

# Data and Seasonal Adjustment

The analysis uses monthly Northern Hemisphere temperature anomalies
from GISTEMP, expressed in degrees Celsius relative to the
1951–1980 reference period. We retain observations from January
1880 to December 2024.

For the retrospective analysis, a fixed seasonal component is
estimated using periodic STL over the selected sample and
subtracted from the observations. Forecast evaluation will use
a separate seasonal adjustment estimated on the training sample only.

```{r load-temperature-data}
data_url <- paste0(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/",
  "MnGianmaria/time-series-analysis/main/",
  "02_temperature_anomalies_and_forecasting/data/gistemp.csv"
)

gistemp_raw <- read.csv(
  data_url,
  skip = 1,
  na.strings = "***",
  check.names = FALSE
)

gistemp_raw <- gistemp_raw[
  gistemp_raw$Year >= 1880 & gistemp_raw$Year <= 2024,
]

month_names <- c(
  "Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr", "May", "Jun",
  "Jul", "Aug", "Sep", "Oct", "Nov", "Dec"
)

monthly_matrix <- as.matrix(gistemp_raw[, month_names])
temperature_values <- as.numeric(t(monthly_matrix))

stopifnot(
  nrow(gistemp_raw) > 0,
  gistemp_raw$Year[1] == 1880,
  tail(gistemp_raw$Year, 1) == 2024,
  all(diff(gistemp_raw$Year) == 1),
  all(is.finite(temperature_values))
)

gistemp_ts <- ts(
  temperature_values,
  start = c(1880, 1),
  frequency = 12
)

seasonal_fit <- stl(
  gistemp_ts,
  s.window = "periodic"
)

y_sa <- gistemp_ts -
  seasonal_fit$time.series[, "seasonal"]

climate_data <- data.frame(
  Date = as.Date(as.yearmon(time(y_sa))),
  Temperature = as.numeric(y_sa)
)
```

The selected sample contains `r length(y_sa)` monthly observations.
Because GISTEMP anomalies already use calendar-month reference
means, STL removes only a residual seasonal pattern; it does
not remove the long-term warming movement.

```{r adjusted-temperature-plot, fig.width=6, fig.height=2, out.width="95%", fig.cap="Seasonally adjusted Northern Hemisphere temperature anomalies, 1880–2024. Periodic STL is applied to the full selected sample for retrospective analysis."}
ggplot(climate_data, aes(x = Date, y = Temperature)) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 0,
    color = "grey70",
    linewidth = 0.3
  ) +
  geom_line(
    color = "#243746",
    linewidth = 0.35
  ) +
  scale_x_date(
    breaks = as.Date(paste0(seq(1880, 2020, 20), "-01-01")),
    date_labels = "%Y"
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Year",
    y = "Temperature anomaly (°C)"
  ) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 9) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(
      color = "#E8E8E8",
      linewidth = 0.2
    ),
    panel.border = element_rect(
      color = "#888888",
      linewidth = 0.3
    )
  )
```

The series displays substantial short-term fluctuations alongside
a sustained rise in recent decades. We therefore consider models
with an evolving latent level, rather than a constant mean.

# Model Specification

We compare two Gaussian dynamic linear models. Unlike an HMM,
whose latent state takes values in a finite set, these models
use a continuous latent state. Changes are represented through
state innovations rather than transitions between discrete regimes.

The random walk plus noise model (RW) specifies an evolving level:

\[
\begin{aligned}
y_t &= \mu_t + \varepsilon_t,
& \varepsilon_t &\sim \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2),\\
\mu_t &= \mu_{t-1} + \eta_t,
& \eta_t &\sim \mathcal{N}(0,\tau^2).
\end{aligned}
\]

The local linear trend model (LLT) adds an evolving slope:

\[
\begin{aligned}
y_t &= \mu_t + \varepsilon_t,
& \varepsilon_t &\sim \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2),\\
\mu_t &= \mu_{t-1} + \beta_{t-1} + \eta_t,
& \eta_t &\sim \mathcal{N}(0,\tau^2),\\
\beta_t &= \beta_{t-1} + \zeta_t,
& \zeta_t &\sim \mathcal{N}(0,\gamma^2).
\end{aligned}
\]

Here, \(\mu_t\) is the latent temperature-anomaly level and
\(\beta_t\) is the local slope, expressed in degrees Celsius
per month. Observation errors and state
innovations are mutually independent, independent over time,
and independent of the initial state.

Both models allow stochastic changes in the level. The LLT
additionally allows the slope to change, although a slope
innovation variance near zero would imply an approximately
constant slope, rather than necessarily a zero slope.

We use Gaussian initial distributions with zero means and
covariance \(10^7 I\), providing a diffuse approximation.
Variance parameters are estimated by maximum likelihood.
Filtering and smoothing intervals then condition on these
estimates and do not incorporate parameter uncertainty.

# Variance Estimation

Variance parameters are estimated by maximum likelihood on the
full seasonally adjusted sample for retrospective analysis.
Optimization uses logarithmic parameters to ensure positivity.

Approximate standard errors are calculated from the numerical
Hessian using the delta method. If the Hessian is not sufficiently
well conditioned, standard errors are left unavailable rather
than reported as reliable estimates.

```{r variance-estimation}
build_rw <- function(log_variances) {
  dlmModPoly(
    order = 1,
    dV = exp(log_variances[1]),
    dW = exp(log_variances[2]),
    m0 = 0,
    C0 = matrix(1e7, 1, 1)
  )
}

build_llt <- function(log_variances) {
  dlmModPoly(
    order = 2,
    dV = exp(log_variances[1]),
    dW = exp(log_variances[2:3]),
    m0 = c(0, 0),
    C0 = diag(1e7, 2)
  )
}

sample_variance <- var(as.numeric(y_sa))

fit_rw <- dlmMLE(
  y_sa,
  parm = log(c(sample_variance, sample_variance / 10)),
  build = build_rw,
  method = "BFGS",
  hessian = TRUE,
  control = list(maxit = 2000, reltol = 1e-10)
)

fit_llt <- dlmMLE(
  y_sa,
  parm = log(c(
    sample_variance,
    sample_variance / 10,
    sample_variance / 100
  )),
  build = build_llt,
  method = "BFGS",
  hessian = TRUE,
  control = list(maxit = 2000, reltol = 1e-10)
)

stopifnot(
  fit_rw$convergence == 0,
  fit_llt$convergence == 0,
  all(is.finite(fit_rw$par)),
  all(is.finite(fit_llt$par))
)

mod_rw <- build_rw(fit_rw$par)
mod_llt <- build_llt(fit_llt$par)

variance_standard_errors <- function(fit) {
  estimates <- exp(fit$par)
  unavailable <- rep(NA_real_, length(estimates))

  H <- (fit$hessian + t(fit$hessian)) / 2

  if (any(!is.finite(H))) {
    return(unavailable)
  }

  eigenvalues <- eigen(H, symmetric = TRUE)$values

  if (min(eigenvalues) <= 1e-8 * max(abs(eigenvalues))) {
    return(unavailable)
  }

  log_covariance <- solve(H)

  estimates * sqrt(diag(log_covariance))
}

rw_estimates <- exp(fit_rw$par)
llt_estimates <- exp(fit_llt$par)

variance_results <- data.frame(
  Model = c("RW", "RW", "LLT", "LLT", "LLT"),
  Parameter = c(
    "Observation variance",
    "Level innovation variance",
    "Observation variance",
    "Level innovation variance",
    "Slope innovation variance"
  ),
  Estimate = c(rw_estimates, llt_estimates),
  SE = c(
    variance_standard_errors(fit_rw),
    variance_standard_errors(fit_llt)
  )
)
```

```{r variance-estimation-table, results='asis'}
variance_display <- variance_results

variance_display$Estimate <- formatC(
  variance_results$Estimate,
  format = "e",
  digits = 3
)

variance_display$SE <- ifelse(
  is.na(variance_results$SE),
  "Unavailable",
  formatC(variance_results$SE, format = "e", digits = 3)
)

slope_row <- which(
  variance_results$Model == "LLT" &
    variance_results$Parameter == "Slope innovation variance"
)

slope_near_boundary <-
  llt_estimates[3] / llt_estimates[1] < 1e-6

if (slope_near_boundary) {
  variance_display$Estimate[slope_row] <- "Near zero"
  variance_display$SE[slope_row] <- "Not reported"
}

kable(
  variance_display,
  format = "latex",
  booktabs = TRUE,
  position = "H",
  row.names = FALSE,
  col.names = c("Model", "Parameter", "Estimate", "Approx. SE"),
  caption = "Full-sample variance estimates. The slope-variance standard error is omitted when its estimate is numerically near the boundary."
)
```

The estimated observation variance is approximately 0.0206
in both models, while the level innovation variance is
approximately 0.0062.

The LLT slope innovation variance is numerically near zero,
indicating little estimated variation in the slope. This does
not imply that the slope itself is zero or establish equivalence
with the RW model. Its approximate standard error is not
reported because the near-boundary estimate makes the
Hessian-based normal approximation unreliable.

# Filtering and Smoothing

For each model, the Kalman filter estimates the latent level
using observations up to the corresponding month. Variance
parameters and seasonal adjustment are estimated on the full
sample, so this is a retrospective analysis rather than a
real-time evaluation.

The shaded bands represent pointwise 95 percent conditional
credible intervals for the latent level, rather than prediction
intervals for observed temperatures.

```{r kalman-filtering}
kfilt_rw <- dlmFilter(y_sa, mod_rw)
kfilt_llt <- dlmFilter(y_sa, mod_llt)

extract_level <- function(state_mean, U, D, model_name) {
  means <- as.matrix(state_mean)[-1, 1]

  covariances <- dlmSvd2var(U, D)
  variances <- vapply(
    covariances[-1],
    function(x) as.numeric(x[1, 1]),
    numeric(1)
  )

  stopifnot(
    length(means) == length(y_sa),
    length(variances) == length(y_sa),
    all(is.finite(means)),
    all(is.finite(variances)),
    all(variances >= 0)
  )

  data.frame(
    Date = climate_data$Date,
    Observed = as.numeric(y_sa),
    Mean = means,
    Variance = variances,
    Lower = means - qnorm(0.975) * sqrt(variances),
    Upper = means + qnorm(0.975) * sqrt(variances),
    Model = model_name
  )
}

filter_rw <- extract_level(
  kfilt_rw$m,
  kfilt_rw$U.C,
  kfilt_rw$D.C,
  "RW"
)

filter_llt <- extract_level(
  kfilt_llt$m,
  kfilt_llt$U.C,
  kfilt_llt$D.C,
  "LLT"
)

filtering_data <- rbind(filter_rw, filter_llt)

filtering_data$Model <- factor(
  filtering_data$Model,
  levels = c("RW", "LLT")
)
```

```{r filtered-levels-plot, fig.width=6, fig.height=3, out.width="95%", fig.cap="Filtered latent levels under the RW and LLT models. Grey lines show seasonally adjusted observations; blue lines and shaded bands show filtered means and pointwise 95 percent conditional state intervals. Both panels use the same axes."}
ggplot(filtering_data, aes(x = Date)) +
  geom_ribbon(
    aes(ymin = Lower, ymax = Upper),
    fill = "#24476B",
    alpha = 0.18
  ) +
  geom_line(
    aes(y = Observed),
    color = "#AAAAAA",
    linewidth = 0.25
  ) +
  geom_line(
    aes(y = Mean),
    color = "#24476B",
    linewidth = 0.4
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~Model, ncol = 1) +
  scale_x_date(
    breaks = as.Date(paste0(seq(1880, 2020, 20), "-01-01")),
    date_labels = "%Y"
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Year",
    y = "Temperature anomaly (°C)"
  ) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 9) +
  theme(
    strip.background = element_rect(
      fill = "#F2F2F2",
      color = NA
    ),
    strip.text = element_text(size = 9),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(
      color = "#E8E8E8",
      linewidth = 0.2
    ),
    panel.spacing = grid::unit(0.8, "lines")
  )
```

Both models track the rise in temperature anomalies in recent
decades while attenuating short-term fluctuations. Their
filtered level estimates and conditional intervals appear
very similar at this plotting scale.

This similarity concerns the estimated levels within the
observed sample; it does not establish equivalence between
the models or equal predictive performance.

Smoothing reconstructs the latent level using the entire observed
series, including observations recorded after each month.
We compare the resulting conditional intervals with those
obtained by filtering.

```{r kalman-smoothing}
ksmooth_rw <- dlmSmooth(kfilt_rw)
ksmooth_llt <- dlmSmooth(kfilt_llt)

smooth_rw <- extract_level(
  ksmooth_rw$s,
  ksmooth_rw$U.S,
  ksmooth_rw$D.S,
  "RW"
)

smooth_llt <- extract_level(
  ksmooth_llt$s,
  ksmooth_llt$U.S,
  ksmooth_llt$D.S,
  "LLT"
)

smoothing_data <- rbind(smooth_rw, smooth_llt)

smoothing_data$Model <- factor(
  smoothing_data$Model,
  levels = c("RW", "LLT")
)

stopifnot(
  all(smooth_rw$Variance <= filter_rw$Variance + 1e-6),
  all(smooth_llt$Variance <= filter_llt$Variance + 1e-6),
  isTRUE(all.equal(
    tail(smooth_rw$Mean, 1),
    tail(filter_rw$Mean, 1)
  )),
  isTRUE(all.equal(
    tail(smooth_llt$Mean, 1),
    tail(filter_llt$Mean, 1)
  ))
)

interval_widths <- data.frame(
  Model = c("RW", "LLT"),
  Filtering = c(
    mean(filter_rw$Upper - filter_rw$Lower),
    mean(filter_llt$Upper - filter_llt$Lower)
  ),
  Smoothing = c(
    mean(smooth_rw$Upper - smooth_rw$Lower),
    mean(smooth_llt$Upper - smooth_llt$Lower)
  )
)
```
```{r initial-state-smoothing}
initial_state_summary <- function(smoothed, model_name) {
  initial_mean <- as.matrix(smoothed$s)[1, 1]
  initial_cov <- dlmSvd2var(
    smoothed$U.S,
    smoothed$D.S
  )[[1]]

  initial_sd <- sqrt(initial_cov[1, 1])

  data.frame(
    Model = model_name,
    Mean = initial_mean,
    Lower = initial_mean - qnorm(0.975) * initial_sd,
    Upper = initial_mean + qnorm(0.975) * initial_sd
  )
}

initial_smoothing <- rbind(
  initial_state_summary(ksmooth_rw, "RW"),
  initial_state_summary(ksmooth_llt, "LLT")
)

kable(
  initial_smoothing,
  format = "latex",
  booktabs = TRUE,
  position = "H",
  digits = 3,
  row.names = FALSE,
  col.names = c("Model", "Mean", "Lower", "Upper"),
  caption = "Smoothed initial level at t = 0: conditional means and 95 percent credible intervals, in degrees Celsius."
)
```

The initial level at \(t=0\), immediately preceding the first
observation, is estimated using the full sample through smoothing.
The figures and mean interval widths below refer to the observed
months, \(t=1,\ldots,T\).

```{r smoothed-levels-plot, fig.width=6, fig.height=3, out.width="95%", fig.cap="Smoothed latent levels under the RW and LLT models. Grey lines show seasonally adjusted observations; blue lines and shaded bands show smoothed means and pointwise 95 percent conditional state intervals. Both panels use the same axes."}

  ) +

  scale_x_date(
    breaks = as.Date(paste0(seq(1880, 2020, 20), "-01-01")),
    date_labels = "%Y"
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Year",
    y = "Temperature anomaly (°C)"
  ) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 9) +
  theme(
    strip.background = element_rect(
      fill = "#F2F2F2",
      color = NA
    ),
    strip.text = element_text(size = 9),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(
      color = "#E8E8E8",
      linewidth = 0.2
    ),
    panel.spacing = grid::unit(0.8, "lines")
  )
```

```{r interval-width-table, results='asis'}
kable(
  interval_widths,
  format = "latex",
  booktabs = TRUE,
  position = "H",
  digits = 3,
  row.names = FALSE,
  col.names = c(
    "Model",
    "Mean filtering width",

  ),
  caption = "Mean width of pointwise 95 percent conditional state intervals, in degrees Celsius."
)
```

The RW and LLT smoothed levels appear very similar at this
plotting scale. Both reconstruct the sustained rise in
temperature anomalies in recent decades while attenuating
short-term fluctuations.

The mean interval width decreases from approximately 0.364 °C
to 0.290 °C for RW and from 0.366 °C to 0.290 °C for LLT.
This reduction reflects the additional information provided
by subsequent observations. At the final observation,
filtering and smoothing coincide.

These are pointwise intervals for the latent level, conditional
on the estimated parameters and seasonal adjustment. They
exclude parameter uncertainty and do not establish real-time
forecasting performance.

# One-Step-Ahead Forecast Evaluation

The final twenty years, January 2005–December 2024, are reserved
for testing. Earlier observations form the training sample.

Periodic STL is fitted to the training sample only. Its estimated
monthly seasonal effects are held fixed and subtracted from
both training and test observations. This avoids using test
observations to estimate the seasonal adjustment.

Both DLMs are then re-estimated on the adjusted training sample.
Their variance parameters remain fixed during testing, while
the state is updated after each new observation. The evaluation
therefore concerns sequential one-month-ahead forecasts,
rather than a twenty-year extrapolation from 2004.

```{r forecast-data-preparation}
temperature_train <- window(
  gistemp_ts,
  end = c(2004, 12)
)

temperature_test <- window(
  gistemp_ts,
  start = c(2005, 1)
)

training_stl <- stl(
  temperature_train,
  s.window = "periodic"
)

seasonal_by_month <- tapply(
  as.numeric(training_stl$time.series[, "seasonal"]),
  cycle(temperature_train),
  mean
)

adjusted_train <- ts(
  as.numeric(temperature_train) -
    seasonal_by_month[as.character(cycle(temperature_train))],
  start = start(temperature_train),
  frequency = 12
)

adjusted_test <- ts(
  as.numeric(temperature_test) -
    seasonal_by_month[as.character(cycle(temperature_test))],
  start = start(temperature_test),
  frequency = 12
)

stopifnot(
  length(adjusted_test) == 20 * 12,
  length(adjusted_train) + length(adjusted_test) ==
    length(gistemp_ts),
  all(is.finite(adjusted_train)),
  all(is.finite(adjusted_test))
)
```

The training sample contains `r length(adjusted_train)` monthly
observations and the test sample contains `r length(adjusted_test)`.
The seasonal effects used here may differ from those estimated
over the full sample for the retrospective analysis.

```{r training-model-estimation}
training_variance <- var(as.numeric(adjusted_train))

fit_rw_train <- dlmMLE(
  adjusted_train,
  parm = log(c(
    training_variance,
    training_variance / 10
  )),
  build = build_rw,
  method = "BFGS",
  control = list(maxit = 2000, reltol = 1e-10)
)

fit_llt_train <- dlmMLE(
  adjusted_train,
  parm = log(c(
    training_variance,
    training_variance / 10,
    training_variance / 100
  )),
  build = build_llt,
  method = "BFGS",
  control = list(maxit = 2000, reltol = 1e-10)
)

stopifnot(
  fit_rw_train$convergence == 0,
  fit_llt_train$convergence == 0,
  all(is.finite(fit_rw_train$par)),
  all(is.finite(fit_llt_train$par))
)

mod_rw_train <- build_rw(fit_rw_train$par)
mod_llt_train <- build_llt(fit_llt_train$par)
```

```{r sequential-test-forecasts}
evaluation_series <- ts(
  c(as.numeric(adjusted_train), as.numeric(adjusted_test)),
  start = start(adjusted_train),
  frequency = 12
)

evaluation_filter_rw <- dlmFilter(
  evaluation_series,
  mod_rw_train
)

evaluation_filter_llt <- dlmFilter(
  evaluation_series,
  mod_llt_train
)

n_train <- length(adjusted_train)
n_test <- length(adjusted_test)
test_indices <- n_train + seq_len(n_test)

pred_rw <- as.numeric(evaluation_filter_rw$f)[test_indices]
pred_llt <- as.numeric(evaluation_filter_llt$f)[test_indices]

err_rw <- as.numeric(adjusted_test) - pred_rw
err_llt <- as.numeric(adjusted_test) - pred_llt

stopifnot(
  length(pred_rw) == n_test,
  length(pred_llt) == n_test,
  all(is.finite(err_rw)),
  all(is.finite(err_llt))
)

forecast_data <- data.frame(
  Date = as.Date(as.yearmon(time(adjusted_test))),
  Observed = as.numeric(adjusted_test),
  RW = pred_rw,
  LLT = pred_llt
)

rmse_results <- data.frame(
  Model = c("RW", "LLT"),
  RMSE = c(
    sqrt(mean(err_rw^2)),
    sqrt(mean(err_llt^2))
  )
)
```

```{r test-forecast-plot, fig.width=6, fig.height=3, out.width="95%", fig.cap="Sequential one-step-ahead forecasts over 2005–2024. Observations are adjusted using seasonal effects estimated on the training sample. Model parameters remain fixed, while states are updated after each observation."}
ggplot(forecast_data, aes(x = Date)) +
  geom_line(
    aes(y = Observed, color = "Observed"),
    linewidth = 0.35
  ) +
  geom_line(
    aes(y = RW, color = "RW"),
    linewidth = 0.5
  ) +
  geom_line(
    aes(y = LLT, color = "LLT"),
    linewidth = 0.5,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "Observed" = "#AAAAAA",
      "RW" = "#24476B",
      "LLT" = "#B36B35"
    ),
    breaks = c("Observed", "RW", "LLT"),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  scale_x_date(
    breaks = as.Date(c(
      "2005-01-01", "2010-01-01",
      "2015-01-01", "2020-01-01", "2025-01-01"
    )),
    date_labels = "%Y"
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Year",
    y = "Temperature anomaly (°C)"
  ) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 9) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(
      color = "#E8E8E8",
      linewidth = 0.2
    )
  )
```

Forecast accuracy is summarized by the root mean squared error:

\[
\mathrm{RMSE}
=
\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_{\mathrm{test}}}
\sum_{t \in \mathrm{test}}(y_t-\hat{y}_{t|t-1})^2}.
\]

Errors are calculated on the seasonally adjusted scale.
Adding the same fixed monthly seasonal effects back to forecasts
and observations leaves these errors unchanged.

```{r test-rmse-table, results='asis'}
kable(
  rmse_results,
  format = "latex",
  booktabs = TRUE,
  position = "H",
  digits = 4,
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Test-sample RMSE for sequential one-step-ahead forecasts, in degrees Celsius."
)
```
The two models produce very similar sequential forecasts,
following the broad increase in temperature anomalies while
missing some sharp monthly fluctuations.

Test RMSE is `r sprintf("%.4f", rmse_results$RMSE[1])` °C
for RW and `r sprintf("%.4f", rmse_results$RMSE[2])` °C
for LLT. The LLT has a slightly lower error on this sample,
but the difference is small and has not been assessed for
statistical significance.

These results concern one-month-ahead prediction with sequential
state updates; they do not establish long-horizon forecasting
accuracy.

We examine test forecast errors using autocorrelation functions,
normal Q-Q plots, and a Ljung–Box test at lag 10. ACF bands
provide approximate pointwise reference limits; the Ljung–Box
test assesses the first ten autocorrelations jointly.

```{r test-error-summary, include=FALSE}
summarize_errors <- function(errors) {
  correlations <- as.numeric(
    acf(errors, lag.max = 40, plot = FALSE)$acf
  )[-1]

  reference_bound <- qnorm(0.975) / sqrt(length(errors))

  c(
    Lag1 = correlations[1],
    Outside = sum(abs(correlations) > reference_bound),
    LjungBoxP = Box.test(
      errors,
      lag = 10,
      type = "Ljung-Box",
      fitdf = 0
    )$p.value
  )
}

error_diagnostics <- rbind(
  RW = summarize_errors(err_rw),
  LLT = summarize_errors(err_llt)
)
```
```{r test-error-diagnostics, fig.width=6.4, fig.height=3.3, out.width="100%", fig.cap="Test forecast error diagnostics for RW and LLT. The upper panels show sample autocorrelations, with lags measured in months and approximate pointwise 95 percent reference bounds. The lower panels show normal Q-Q plots of errors in degrees Celsius."}
local({
  old_par <- par(no.readonly = TRUE)
  on.exit(par(old_par))

  par(
    mfrow = c(2, 2),
    mar = c(3.5, 3.8, 2.5, 1),
    mgp = c(2.2, 0.7, 0),
    cex = 0.8
  )

  acf(
    err_rw,
    lag.max = 40,
    main = "",
    xlab = "Lag (months)",
    ylab = "ACF",
    col = "#24476B"
  )
  title(main = "A  RW: ACF", line = 1)

  acf(
    err_llt,
    lag.max = 40,
    main = "",
    xlab = "Lag (months)",
    ylab = "ACF",
    col = "#24476B"
  )
  title(main = "B  LLT: ACF", line = 1)

  qqnorm(
    err_rw,
    main = "",
    xlab = "Theoretical quantiles",
    ylab = "Sample quantiles (°C)",
    pch = 16,
    cex = 0.55,
    col = "#24476B"
  )
  qqline(err_rw, col = "#B36B35", lwd = 1)
  title(main = "C  RW: Normal Q-Q", line = 1)

  qqnorm(
    err_llt,
    main = "",
    xlab = "Theoretical quantiles",
    ylab = "Sample quantiles (°C)",
    pch = 16,
    cex = 0.55,
    col = "#24476B"
  )
  qqline(err_llt, col = "#B36B35", lwd = 1)
  title(main = "D  LLT: Normal Q-Q", line = 1)
})
```
Both models leave substantial serial dependence in their
forecast errors. Lag-one autocorrelation is approximately
0.24 for each model. Among the first forty lags, 21 exceed
the pointwise reference bounds for RW and 20 for LLT.
The Ljung–Box test at lag 10 gives p-values below \(10^{-6}\)
for both models, providing strong evidence against the
absence of autocorrelation over these lags.

The normal Q-Q plots are broadly consistent with a Gaussian
distribution, without pronounced departures from the reference
lines. This visual assessment does not establish normality
or independence.

The LLT does not materially improve these diagnostics relative
to the RW model.

# Discussion and Limitations

The RW and LLT models represent temperature anomalies through
a continuous-valued latent level. Both track the sustained
increase in recent decades and produce very similar filtered
and smoothed estimates. Smoothing reduces conditional state
uncertainty by incorporating subsequent observations.

The full-sample LLT slope innovation variance is numerically
near zero, suggesting an approximately constant slope within
this fitted specification. This does not imply a zero slope
or exact equivalence with RW. Test RMSE values are practically
identical, so RW provides a more parsimonious representation
with comparable sequential one-step-ahead accuracy.

For representing gradual long-term movements, the evolving
levels and slopes of DLMs offer a more direct description
than a level-based HMM, which approximates such movements
through switches between discrete states. HMMs instead offer
an interpretable classification into a small number of fitted
states, although frequent switches can weaken their
interpretation as persistent regimes. These are differences
in representation; no predictive comparison with HMMs is
performed here, and neither approach identifies physical
climate mechanisms.

Both frameworks use a latent Markov process and assume
conditionally independent observations given the state
sequence. Parameters are estimated by maximum likelihood,
and recursive filtering and smoothing provide latent-state
distributions. HMM forward-backward smoothing and Kalman
smoothing use the full sample to obtain marginal distributions.
Viterbi decoding instead selects a single most likely
discrete state sequence.

The test errors retain substantial serial dependence:
lag-one autocorrelation is approximately 0.24 for both models,
and Ljung–Box tests at lag 10 give p-values below \(10^{-6}\).
The LLT does not resolve this limitation. Normal Q-Q plots
are broadly consistent with Gaussian errors, but this does
not establish independence or validate the full specification.

State intervals condition on estimated parameters and seasonal
adjustment, excluding their uncertainty. The near-boundary
slope variance also makes its Hessian-based standard error
unreliable, so that standard error is not reported.

Finally, evaluation uses one chronological split and a fixed
seasonal pattern estimated on the training sample. The results
concern sequential one-month-ahead forecasts using revised
historical data; they do not establish long-horizon accuracy
or performance with data available in real time.
